note: A man betrothed a woman with a blue marble stone, and Rav Hisda checked whether it was worth a peruta. The man's mother said it had been worth a peruta on the day of the betrothal, but Rav Hisda said she could not make the woman forbidden to another man. He compared it to Yehudit, Rabbi Hiyya's wife, who suffered painful childbirths and claimed her mother said she had been betrothed to someone else as a child; Rabbi Hiyya told her that her mother could not forbid her to him. When the Sages pointed out that there were witnesses in Idit who knew the stone's value that day, Rav Hisda answered that they were not here.
why: Shmuel had ruled that a betrothal with a cheap item may still count, since it might be worth a peruta elsewhere; the Gemara shows Rav Hisda rejecting that view. Afterwards Abaye and Rava disagree, and the Sages avoided marrying into the woman's family.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The judge who ruled on the betrothal with the blue marble stone.

people.name: Yehudit
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's wife, who suffered painful childbirths and wished to leave him.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: Yehudit's husband, who told her that her mother's claim could not forbid her to him.

terms.meaning: The smallest coin; an object given for betrothal must be worth at least this much.
The first stage of Jewish marriage, made by giving the woman something of value; after it she is bound to the man and forbidden to others.

note: Rabbi Yehuda from India was a convert who had no heirs. When he fell ill, Mar Zutra came to visit him, and when he saw that the sick man was about to die, he told the man's slave: Take off my shoes and carry them to my house. By having the slave serve him, Mar Zutra meant to claim the slave as soon as the owner died. Some say the slave was an adult, and the Gemara sums up: one departed to death, and the other departed to life.
why: The discussion has just said a master acquires a slave when the slave does work for him, such as lifting him; Mar Zutra uses that method. Afterwards the Gemara asks whether, if the slave was a minor, he even needed to hurry.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda from India
people.about: A convert with no heirs, who was dying.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: A Sage who visited him and acquired his slave before he died.

terms.meaning: When a convert with no Jewish heirs dies, his property is ownerless, and the first person to take possession of it acquires it.

note: Rav Yosef said that if Aher, the former Sage Elisha ben Avuya, had read the verse "that it may go well with you" as referring to the World-to-Come, as his grandson Rabbi Ya'akov did, he would not have sinned. The Gemara asks what made him sin. Some say he saw a son climb to a roof at his father's command, send away a mother bird as the Torah requires, and then die. Others say he saw the tongue of Hutzpit the disseminator, who had been executed by the government, lying in the street and being dragged by a pig, and said: Shall a mouth that produced pearls lap up dirt? For this he went out and sinned.
why: The Gemara has been defending Rabbi Ya'akov's teaching that the reward for mitzvot comes in the World-to-Come, not in this world, citing a son who died returning from exactly these mitzvot; Aher is the one who drew the opposite conclusion.

people.name: Aher
people.about: Literally Other, the name given to the former Sage Elisha ben Avuya after he sinned.

people.name: Rabbi Ya'akov
people.about: Aher's daughter's son, who taught that the promised reward is in the World-to-Come.

people.name: Hutzpit the disseminator
people.about: A Sage executed by the government, whose tongue Aher saw in the street.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who says Aher would not have sinned had he read the verse as Rabbi Ya'akov did.

terms.meaning: The life after this one, where, in Rabbi Ya'akov's teaching, the reward for mitzvot is paid.
A Torah commandment to send off the mother before taking eggs or chicks from a nest; like honoring parents, it is promised long life.
The person who repeated a Sage's lecture aloud so the whole audience could hear it.

note: A blind man used to review mishnayot with Mar Shmuel. One day he was late, so Mar Shmuel sent a messenger to bring him. The two missed each other on different roads, and the messenger reached the blind man's house. He came back and reported that he had seen the man's wife committing adultery. The blind man asked Mar Shmuel what to do, and Mar Shmuel told him: If this messenger is trusted by you, go and divorce her; if not, do not divorce her.
why: Abaye and Rava disagree whether a single witness is believed when he says a man's wife committed adultery; Abaye tells this case as his proof, and Rava answers that Mar Shmuel meant trusted like two witnesses.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage who tells this case as proof for his view.

people.name: Mar Shmuel
people.about: The teacher with whom the blind man reviewed mishnayot, who answered his question.

terms.meaning: Teachings of the Mishna, the earliest written collection of Jewish law, which students memorized and reviewed aloud.
